title: Materials: Ceramics, Polymers and Composites
strapline: Choosing the right material for the job, and justifying it with properties.
bigIdea: Materials are chosen, not found. Every engineering choice is a trade-off between properties, cost and environmental impact.
priorKnowledge: Unit 3: properties of metals and non-metals.
futureLearning: GCSE: polymers and their structures, nanoparticles, life cycle assessment, alloys.

misconceptions.whyItSticks: One everyday word covers dozens of polymers.
misconceptions.addressIt: Compare the properties of four named polymers and match each to a use they could not swap.

misconceptions.whyItSticks: Strength is the most familiar property word.
misconceptions.addressIt: Use a selection task where the best answer requires flexibility or low density, not strength.

misconceptions.misconception: Composites are just mixtures, so they are nothing new.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Composites are physically combined, not bonded.
misconceptions.addressIt: Test concrete with and without reinforcement; the composite property exceeds either component alone.

misconceptions.misconception: Ceramics are always fragile and only used for crockery.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Broken mugs are the reference point.
misconceptions.addressIt: Show ceramic uses in body armour and heat shields; distinguish brittle from weak.

keyVocabulary.definition: A hard, brittle, heat-resistant material made by firing a non-metal mineral.
A material made of long chain molecules formed from many repeating units.
A material made from two or more materials with different properties, combined to give better properties overall.
Breaks suddenly without bending or stretching first.

practicals.title: Comparing material properties
apparatus: samples: steel, aluminium, ceramic tile, rigid and flexible polymer, wood, carbon fibre offcut
newton meter or masses and clamp
measuring cylinder for volume by displacement
hazards: Sharp edges on broken ceramic and metal offcuts
control: Place a cushioned tray beneath suspended masses; feet clear
Goggles when loading to failure; samples with filed edges only

practicals.title: Testing a composite against its components
hazards: Plaster sets exothermically and must never be moulded around body parts
control: Never mould plaster on hands or fingers under any circumstances
Mix in a well-ventilated area; wear goggles and avoid raising dust
practicals.timing: 30 minutes to make, 30 minutes to test in a later lesson

formative: Material selection cards: justify a choice against three stated requirements.
Property vocabulary discrimination: strong, hard, tough, brittle, stiff.
Peer critique of a material recommendation.

summative.title: Materials selection task
summative.style: 20 marks: a design brief requiring a justified material choice supported by property data and one environmental consideration.
summative.markSchemeNotes: Credit trade-offs. A top-band answer names a drawback of the chosen material and explains why it is acceptable here.

lessons.title: Properties and how we measure them

sequence.detail: Property vocabulary check: distinguish strong, hard, tough and brittle.
Define each property operationally — how would you measure it? Fair test requirements established.
Test seven samples for density, conductivity and flexibility; tabulate results.
Compare group results; discuss variation and precision.

keyQuestions: Is glass strong or brittle? Can it be both?
What must you keep the same to compare flexibility fairly?
support: Results table with units supplied; density calculation frame.
challenge: Rank the materials by strength-to-weight ratio and comment on the result.
lessons.homework: Complete the results table and write two comparative conclusions.
lessons.exitTicket: Give the difference between brittle and weak.

lessons.title: Ceramics and polymers
objectives: Describe the properties of ceramics and polymers
retrieval: Which material had the lowest density?

sequence.detail: Property definitions and last lesson's data recalled.
Ceramics: how they are made and why they are hard, brittle and heat resistant. Polymers: chain molecules, and how chain arrangement changes flexibility.
Match eight materials to uses; justify each with two properties.
Surface and correct the 'plastic is one material' misconception using four named polymers.

keyQuestions: Why is a ceramic used for a heat shield rather than a metal?
Why is a carrier bag polymer unsuitable for a kettle?
support: Property cards supplied alongside the use cards.
challenge: Explain how the structure of a polymer chain accounts for its flexibility.
lessons.homework: Research and describe one ceramic and one polymer, with uses and properties.
lessons.exitTicket: Give one property that makes ceramics suitable for oven dishes.

lessons.title: Composites
objectives: Explain why a composite outperforms its components

sequence.detail: Matrix and reinforcement explained; reinforced concrete, carbon fibre and plywood as examples.
Make and test plaster beams with and without fibre reinforcement; record the load at failure.
Explain the results: which component provides which property?

keyQuestions: Which part resists compression and which resists being pulled apart?
Why not just use more of the stronger material?
support: Results table supplied; teacher pre-makes one set of beams.
challenge: Explain why carbon fibre is used in aircraft despite costing far more than aluminium.
lessons.homework: Explain how reinforced concrete works, with a labelled diagram.
lessons.exitTicket: Define a composite in one sentence.

lessons.title: Material selection task
objectives: Select a material for a design brief
Justify the choice using property data and environmental impact

sequence.detail: Design brief: choose a material for a named product; justify with data; address recyclability.
Structured peer feedback against the mark scheme.
Model a top-band answer; pupils identify what made it stronger.

keyQuestions: What is the drawback of your chosen material, and why is it acceptable here?
How does recyclability change your recommendation?
support: Property data table provided; writing frame with four required sections.
challenge: Compare two viable materials and justify the trade-off explicitly.
lessons.homework: Improve the response following peer feedback.
lessons.exitTicket: Name one trade-off you had to make in your choice.
